label: Voronoi Algorithm
notes: Start with the operational problem: many places in the plane need to know which input site is closest. Chapter 7 first defines the Voronoi diagram and its basic geometric structure, then uses those properties to motivate an algorithm. The arc of the lecture is that a nearest-neighbor partition is not just a picture; its edges, vertices, and dual graph give algorithmic certificates.

label: Assignment Model
notes: Give the definition as an assignment rule, not as a drawing rule. A point belongs to the cell of p_i when p_i is at least as close as every other site. The colored regions are the maximal areas where the answer to the nearest-site query is constant. Boundaries record ties, which is why bisectors are the real skeleton of the diagram.

label: Half-Plane Cell
notes: Derive convexity from one comparison. Squaring distances cancels the quadratic terms, so the inequality between p_i and p_j is linear in x. Intersect that half-plane over all j and the whole cell appears. This is a useful pause because it links Voronoi cells back to the half-plane language students already saw earlier in the course.

label: Structure Complexity
notes: Reframe the diagram as a planar graph. The faces correspond to sites, the edges to two-site ties, and the vertices to three-site ties. Under the usual no-four-cocircular assumption, internal vertices have degree three. Euler's formula then gives the important algorithmic message: even though every pair of sites has a bisector, only a linear number of bisector pieces survive in the final diagram.

label: Empty Circle
notes: Use empty circles as the bridge from structure to algorithms. If a center is on an edge, two sites are equally close and no site is closer, so the corresponding circle is empty and touches two sites. At a vertex, three cells meet and the circle touches three sites. These certificates will reappear as circle events in Fortune's sweep and as the Delaunay dual later.

label: Beach Line
notes: Explain the beach line as a moving frontier of uncertainty. The sweep line has processed sites above it. A point on the beach line is equally close to a processed site and to the sweep line, so parabolic arcs form the frontier. The important invariant is not the shape of a parabola by itself; it is that the completed diagram above the beach line will not be changed by sites still below the sweep line.

label: Site Event
notes: At a site event, the sweep line reaches a site for the first time. The new site's parabola initially has no width, but immediately after the event it cuts into the beach line and splits one existing arc into two pieces. The breakpoints on either side of the new arc are the moving ends of a Voronoi edge between the new site and the site whose arc was split.

label: Circle Event
notes: Circle events are the moment where empty-circle geometry becomes an algorithmic event. Three neighboring arcs may define a circle through their sites. When the sweep reaches the bottom of that circle, the middle arc has no future interval on the beach line and disappears. The two breakpoints collide at the center of the circle, which is exactly the Voronoi vertex to record.

label: Data Structures
notes: This is the engineering slide. The event queue determines the next sweep action. The beach-line tree lets us find, split, and remove arcs in logarithmic time. The DCEL is where geometric events become a persistent subdivision. Emphasize that invalid circle events are normal: when an arc is split before its predicted disappearance, the old event must be marked inactive or removed.

label: Degeneracy Clinic
notes: Make degeneracy feel like part of the specification, not an embarrassment. Equal sweep heights require a stable event order. Cocircular sites mean several Voronoi edges meet at one geometric point rather than at a chain of distinct degree-three vertices. Small numerical errors can leave zero-length edge records. The goal is to preserve the combinatorial meaning even when the generic-position story is not literally true.

label: Segment Sites
notes: Move from point sites to segment sites by asking where the nearest point on a segment lies. If the perpendicular projection lands inside the segment, distance behaves like distance to a line. If the closest point is an endpoint, the endpoint behaves like a point site. That mixture explains why segment-site Voronoi diagrams contain both straight and curved pieces.

label: Retraction Disc Motion
notes: The segment-site diagram becomes useful in disc motion planning. Inflate obstacles by the disc radius, or equivalently track the disc center among obstacle features. A path can be retracted toward the Voronoi skeleton because that skeleton keeps locally maximal clearance from obstacles. The continuous planning problem is then represented by connectors to a clearance graph and graph search on that skeleton.

label: Farthest Cells
notes: Reverse the nearest-site inequality and students should immediately notice a different geometry. Interior points of the input set cannot win far away, and in fact only convex-hull sites have nonempty farthest cells. The farthest diagram is unbounded and tree-like because it records which hull point is most extreme in each direction.

label: Randomized Farthest
notes: For farthest diagrams, the convex hull is the gatekeeper. A randomized incremental construction can ignore insertions that stay interior, because they have no farthest cell. When a point becomes part of the hull, the affected portion of the farthest tree is local to the newly exposed hull chain. This is the same randomized-incremental mindset as earlier, now applied to a different diagram.

label: Annulus Candidates
notes: The annulus problem combines the two diagrams. For a chosen center, the outer radius is determined by a farthest site and the inner radius by a nearest site. We want the smallest difference between those two radii. The candidate centers occur where the responsible nearest and farthest features can change, so the nearest and farthest Voronoi structures give a finite search framework.

label: Delaunay Bridge
notes: Close by naming the two durable ideas. First, Voronoi diagrams generalize whenever a distance or site model gives meaningful nearest features. Second, the point-site diagram has a dual: if two cells share an edge, connect the two sites. Empty-circle certificates explain why that graph is the Delaunay structure we will use for triangulations and proximity reasoning.
